:::note[Written against main]
This page follows `main` at 9d25dc1, and it differs from the copy in HotLoop 4.17.0, the latest release. Parts of it may be newer than what you have installed. The [release notes](/releases/) say what moved.
:::

The chart deploys two workloads: the gateway (a Deployment, it holds no durable
state of its own) and TimescaleDB (a StatefulSet with a volume). That is the
default. `database.type` picks another database: plain PostgreSQL, or SQLite,
which is no second workload at all ([SQLite](#sqlite), below).

## Install

Through the EmberNET dashboard's App Store, or directly:

```bash
helm install hotloop ./charts/hotloop \
  --namespace hotloop --create-namespace
```

Or from the chart repository, which is also the URL the App Store points at:

```bash
helm repo add hotloop https://hotloop.io/hotloop
helm install hotloop hotloop/hotloop \
  --namespace hotloop --create-namespace
```

That second form works from 4.16.0 on, the first release published as
`hotloop`. The last one before it was `industrial-iot` 4.3.1, under the old
name, and upgrading from it is its own procedure: see "Upgrading from 4.3.1"
in the README's 4.16.0 notes. The old repository address,
`https://embernet-ai.github.io/industrial-iot/`, is a 404.

A bare install works. The chart generates a database password and an MCP token
into the release Secret and reuses them across upgrades, so nothing needs
supplying and an upgrade does not rotate the password out from under a running
database.

Reaching it needs no ingress and no subdomain. The dashboard discovers the app
by its store labels and proxies it at the in-cluster address:

```
<release>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:8080
```

To look at it directly:

```bash
kubectl -n hotloop port-forward svc/hotloop 8080:8080
```

## Values worth setting

### Auth

Since 4.4.0. See [docs/AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/) for the full model; this is the chart
side of it.

```yaml
auth:
  enabled: true    # the default; requires a login
  insecure: false  # set true only for a deployment truly isolated behind the
                    # dashboard's own NetworkPolicy -- see AUTH.md
```

With `enabled: true` (the default) the chart generates an admin account into
the release Secret on first install, the same way it generates the database
password and the MCP token, and reuses it across upgrades:

```bash
kubectl get secret hotloop -n hotloop \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.admin-password}' | base64 -d
```

Setting `auth.admin.password` explicitly overrides the generated one. Neither
this nor a Helm upgrade ever overwrites a password an operator has since
changed through the UI, see `EnsureAdminUser`'s comment in
`internal/store/users.go`.

### Safety

The values that decide whether this pod can move machinery.

```yaml
safety:
  allowWrites: false      # the master switch -- off by default since 4.4.0
  allowMcpWrites: false   # a narrowing of it, for agents
  confirmWrites: true     # the UI asks before writing
```

Writes are off by default. A tag is read-only until its own `writable` flag is
set regardless, a value outside the tag's configured range is refused (never
clamped: sending 250 when somebody typed 500 is quietly doing something else),
and every attempt, **including every refusal**, is recorded with the actor and
the source. But a fresh install shouldn't need all three of those to line up
before it's safe, so the master switch itself starts closed.

To turn writes on once the deployment has been reviewed:

```yaml
safety:
  allowWrites: true
  allowMcpWrites: false  # let operators write while agents may not
```

### Historian

```yaml
historian:
  retentionDays: 90     # 0 keeps everything until the volume fills
  useTimescale: true

logbook:
  retentionDays: 90     # entity state changes; 0 keeps everything (see LOGBOOK.md)

database:
  postgresql:
    persistence:
      size: 20Gi
      storageClass: longhorn
```

Sizing is driven by tag count, scan rate and deadbands. A thousand tags at one
second with no deadbands is roughly 86 million rows a day; the same plant with
sensible deadbands is usually an order of magnitude less. Set deadbands before
buying storage.

`useTimescale: false` forces the native-partitioning path, which is what running
against a plain PostgreSQL looks like. Useful for reproducing an edge deployment.

**When the TimescaleDB image changes.** The image carries every older version's
library, so a database made on an older image keeps running on the new one, but
on the old extension version, and it stays there until someone runs
`ALTER EXTENSION timescaledb UPDATE`. The Gateway does that on start: it compares
the installed version with the one the server ships and, if they differ, runs
the update as the first statement of a fresh connection (TimescaleDB refuses it
in a session that has already loaded the old version). The log says
`timescaledb extension updated from=... to=...`. That needs a superuser, which the
bundled database's user is. Against an external or managed database where it
isn't, you get a warning with the command to run, and history keeps working on
the old version in the meantime. Only happens with `useTimescale` on and
migrations running on start (`HOTLOOP_DB_MIGRATE`, on by default).

### Polling

```yaml
runtime:
  defaultPollIntervalMs: 1000
  minPollIntervalMs: 100      # a floor applied to every device
  timeoutMs: 10000
  maxConcurrentPolls: 32
```

`minPollIntervalMs` is enforced rather than trusted. A 10 ms poll against a
serial gateway is a denial of service with extra steps.

### OPC UA client

```yaml
opcuaClient:
  persistence:
    enabled: true      # off by default
    size: 64Mi
```

A device that connects to a secured OPC UA server, or that logs in with a user
name and password the server needs encrypted, keeps a certificate and a trust
store of approved server certificates (`HOTLOOP_OPCUA_CLIENT_PKI_DIR`,
`/data/opcua-client-pki`). Turn this on before adding such a device: the root
filesystem is read-only, so without the volume the device reports an error that
says so instead of connecting with certificates that would be lost at the next
restart. It is off by default because it adds a PersistentVolumeClaim to an
existing install, which stays Pending on a cluster with no default StorageClass.
Anonymous devices on an unsecured channel do not use it. Approving a server's
certificate, and everything else about these devices, is in
[PROTOCOLS.md](/iot/protocols/#opc-ua-security-and-credentials).

### Networking

```yaml
networkPolicy:
  enabled: true
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: dashboard-system
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
```

Narrow ingress to the dashboard's namespace once it is known. Egress is
deliberately unrestricted: this app exists to reach equipment at addresses
nobody can enumerate in advance, and an egress policy that silently blocks a
poll looks like a broken driver rather than a firewall rule.

### Edge deployments

The app image is built for amd64 and arm64, and TimescaleDB 2.30.1-pg16 is
multi-arch, so the historian is not what stops an edge install.

```yaml
resources:
  requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
  limits:   {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi}

database:
  postgresql:
    persistence: {size: 5Gi}
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi}
      limits:   {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}

historian:
  retentionDays: 30

nodeSelector:
  kubernetes.io/arch: arm64
```

### Publishing upstream over Sparkplug

An edge Gateway can also publish everything it reads to a central one, as a
Sparkplug B edge node. See [EDGE-PUBLISH.md](/edge/edge-publish/) for what it
publishes and how the forward queue behaves; this is the chart side.

```yaml
edgePublish:
  enabled: true
  broker: tcp://central.example.local:1883
  group: Plant1
  node: press-line-3          # empty uses the release name
  username: press-line-3
  existingSecret: central-mqtt # key "password", or set secretKey
  tls: false
  queueMaxBytes: 536870912     # 512 MiB; the default is 64 MiB, and 0 is unbounded
  persistence:
    size: 1Gi
```

What turning it on changes, and why:

- **A 1Gi PVC for the forward queue**, mounted at `/data/edge-publish`. That's
  where readings pile up while the uplink is down, so it has to outlive the pod.
  `persistence.enabled: false` puts it on an emptyDir instead, which survives a
  container restart and nothing else.
- **The Deployment rolls with `Recreate`.** The queue is one file with a lock
  on it. A rolling update starts the new pod first, the new pod can't open the
  queue, it never goes ready, and the rollout sits there forever. Recreate
  stops the old one first; you lose a few seconds of polling per upgrade.
- **`replicaCount` has to be 1**, and the chart refuses to render otherwise.
  Two replicas would be two publishers claiming one Sparkplug node.
- **The node id defaults to the release name**, not the pod's host name. The
  host name changes on every rollout, and a Sparkplug host would see a brand
  new edge node each time.

The password never goes in a plaintext default. Leave `password` and
`existingSecret` empty for an anonymous broker and no Secret is created; set
`password` and the chart puts it in `<release>-edge-publish`; set
`existingSecret` to use one you manage.

### External database

```yaml
database:
  postgresql:
    enabled: false
    auth:
      existingSecret: my-db-credentials
      secretKey: password
  external:
    host: timescale.plant.local
    port: 5432
    database: industrial
    username: industrial
  sslMode: require
```

The app detects TimescaleDB and promotes `tag_history` to a hypertable when the
extension is present. Against a plain PostgreSQL it falls back to native range
partitioning instead of failing.

The decision is recorded and **sticky**. A database created as a hypertable
refuses to start against a server without the extension rather than silently
writing somewhere else, if you see that error, you have pointed the app at a
different database than it was built on.

### SQLite

The database is a setting, not an image. Every product runs on SQLite,
Postgres or TimescaleDB out of the same binary (IoT skips TimescaleDB, see
below):

| Variable | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_DB_TYPE` | `postgres` | `postgres` or `sqlite`. TimescaleDB is `postgres` with the extension on the server |
| `HOTLOOP_DB_PATH` | `/data/hotloop.db` | The SQLite file. Only SQLite reads it |

SQLite is the pure Go one (`modernc.org/sqlite`), compiled into every image, so
there's no second container, no 300 MB Postgres image on an SD card, and the
arm builds stay static. Put the file on a volume that outlives the container,
and on a Pi put that volume on a USB SSD. A historian writing to an SD card all
day is how you buy a lot of SD cards.

What's the same: every table, every column, every feature. What's different:

- History is one table with an index, not partitions or a hypertable, and
  retention deletes old rows instead of dropping months. A site with years of
  history at one second wants Postgres or TimescaleDB, and moving there is a
  backup and a restore (BACKUP.md).
- One writer at a time. SQLite takes turns on writes and reads alongside them
  (WAL), which is plenty for one HotLoop and an `--mcp-stdio` helper beside it
  on the same file. It isn't for two replicas on network storage: SQLite on NFS
  corrupts, so a SQLite deployment is one pod with a local volume.
- Commits are `synchronous=FULL`: when the API says it saved, it's on disk,
  power cut or not.

**HotLoop IoT** defaults to 30 days of history (`HOTLOOP_HISTORIAN_RETENTION_DAYS`
still wins when it's set) and never builds a hypertable: TimescaleDB is part of
Edge and Gateway. Set `HOTLOOP_HISTORIAN_TIMESCALE=true` on IoT and it says so
at start and runs on plain partitions. A database moved down from an Edge or a
Gateway that already has a hypertable keeps it and keeps working.

#### Picking the database in the chart

One value, `database.type`, and each product takes the ones it runs on:

| `database.type` | What gets deployed | IoT | Edge | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `timescaledb` | The app and TimescaleDB (a StatefulSet and its volume). History in a hypertable | refused | default | default |
| `postgresql` | The app and plain PostgreSQL 16 (a StatefulSet and its volume). History in native partitions | default | yes | yes |
| `sqlite` | The app alone, with the database file on a volume of its own | yes | yes | yes |

```bash
helm install hotloop hotloop/hotloop-iot --namespace hotloop --create-namespace   --set database.type=sqlite
```

Asking IoT for `timescaledb` fails the install and says what IoT runs on
(`database.type is "timescaledb", and HotLoop IoT runs on sqlite, postgresql`),
and the form in the App Store doesn't offer it. `helm lint` does not catch it
(helm 3.22 lints it clean), so the render is what refuses. Leaving
`database.type` out is the product's own default, so an upgrade with
`--reuse-values` from before the key existed keeps the database it had.

`sqlite` renders:

- `HOTLOOP_DB_TYPE=sqlite` and `HOTLOOP_DB_PATH=/data/db/hotloop.db`, and none
  of the Postgres connection settings. No database pod, no database password
  in the Secret, no init container waiting for one.
- A PersistentVolumeClaim named `<release>-db` (`database.sqlite.persistence`:
  `size`, `storageClass`, `accessMode`, 10Gi and the cluster default to start),
  mounted at `/data/db`. The directory, not the file: SQLite keeps a `-wal` and
  a `-shm` beside the database. Put it on local storage; SQLite on NFS
  corrupts.
- The Deployment on `Recreate`, not a rolling update, because the volume is
  `ReadWriteOnce` and the file has one writer. `replicaCount` above 1 fails
  the install.

The NetworkPolicy is unchanged and on: the app's own policy still applies, and
the database policy is only rendered when there is a database pod to protect.

Changing `database.type` on a release that already has data does not move the
data. The new database starts empty, so moving a plant between databases is a
backup and a restore (BACKUP.md), the same as with the variable. In particular
a database that was made as a TimescaleDB hypertable refuses to start against
plain PostgreSQL, so do not flip an existing Edge or Gateway from `timescaledb`
to `postgresql` and expect it to come up.

#### Picking the database in Quadlet

Each product's directory under `deploy/quadlet/` has the PostgreSQL or
TimescaleDB files as they were, and a `sqlite/` directory beside them:
`hotloop.container` and `hotloop-data.volume`, the app alone with the file at
`/data/hotloop.db` on the `hotloop-data` volume. It follows `:stable` and rolls
back a bad update the same way. Install those two files instead of the others
(they use the same unit names), and make two secrets rather than three: there
is no database password. [`deploy/quadlet/README.md`](/install/quadlet/)
has the steps.

For plain Postgres partitions on Edge or the Gateway under Quadlet, keep the
TimescaleDB unit and add `Environment=HOTLOOP_HISTORIAN_TIMESCALE=false` to
`hotloop.container`. IoT's unit already runs plain PostgreSQL.

### The device credential key

```yaml
secretKey:
  enabled: true
  existingSecret: ""     # or a Secret you manage, with the key under secret.key
```

Device passwords (a UniFi console login, an OPC UA or MQTT password, HTTP API
keys) are encrypted in the database with this key, so a dump or a backup holds
ciphertext. Out of the box the chart generates one into `<release>-secret-key`
on the first install, keeps it across upgrades, and keeps it on `helm
uninstall` too (`helm.sh/resource-policy: keep`), because a database kept on its
volume is no use for its credentials without it. It's mounted as a file and
passed as `HOTLOOP_SECRET_KEY_FILE`, never as an environment variable.

Back the Secret up separately from the database backups: a key sitting next to
the backups it protects protects nothing. To bring your own, `hotloop
gen-secret-key` prints one. Outside Kubernetes, write it to a file only HotLoop
can read and point `HOTLOOP_SECRET_KEY_FILE` at it. Without a key HotLoop runs,
says in its startup log that device passwords are stored as typed, and refuses
to save a UniFi console. Credentials already stored are encrypted the first time
it starts with a key. See [BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/#device-credentials-and-the-secret-key)
for what that means for a restore.

## Configuration, and what the Settings screen can change

Almost every setting comes from an environment variable that the chart sets from
a Helm value. That is the right place for it: configuration deciding whether this
process can command machinery belongs in the deployment, reviewed, not in a form
on a web page.

The **Settings** screen shows all of it, every setting, its effective value,
whether it came from the database, an environment variable or the built-in
default, and the variable that changes it. Most of it is read-only, which is the
point: the question it answers is "why is it doing that, and what do I change?"

Four settings are plant identity rather than behavior, and are editable there.
They are stored in the database and take effect immediately, because a plant is
renamed far more often than it is redeployed:

| setting | variable it overrides |
|---|---|
| Plant name | `HOTLOOP_PLANT_NAME` |
| Site ID | `HOTLOOP_SITE_ID` |
| Timezone | `HOTLOOP_TIMEZONE` |
| Confirm before writing | `HOTLOOP_CONFIRM_WRITES` |

A stored value wins over the environment variable, so the chart's value becomes
the starting point rather than the last word. A timezone the machine cannot
resolve is refused rather than accepted and quietly ignored, which would leave
every timestamp falling back to UTC with nothing saying why.

The same goes for the deployment's own value. If `HOTLOOP_TIMEZONE` (or `TZ`,
when that's unset) names a zone that won't load, HotLoop refuses to start and
the error names the variable and the value. It used to shrug and run on UTC.
Reports, schedules and shift times all run on the plant's clock, and a guess
hours off is worse than a pod that says why it won't come up.

The site's location is `HOTLOOP_SITE_LATITUDE` and `HOTLOOP_SITE_LONGITUDE`
(chart: `plant.latitude`, `plant.longitude`), decimal degrees, north and east
positive. Sunrise, sunset and the sun's entities and triggers are worked out
from them on the box ([SUN.md](/iot/sun/)). Both or neither, and a bad one stops
startup with the variable named. The Settings screen shows them read-only:
rules fire on a sunrise, so moving it is a deploy.

**The safety switches are not editable and will not be.** `HOTLOOP_ALLOW_WRITES` is
the master control over whether this process can command equipment; a control
that can be switched back on from the same browser session that issues the writes
is not a control. `HOTLOOP_HISTORIAN_RETENTION_DAYS` is likewise deployment-only, the retention policy is applied to the database at startup, so a field on a
screen would look like it worked and move no data. The endpoint refuses any key
outside the editable set **by name**, rather than ignoring it.

One limitation, stated because the screen states it too: the MCP server builds
its instructions at startup, so it advertises the plant name it booted with until
the pod restarts. Everything else picks a rename up on the next request.

## Upgrading from 3.x

**This is a replacement, not an upgrade.** 3.x was a different product. There is no migration path for its data, because it shares no data model with a tag historian.

```bash
helm uninstall hotloop -n hotloop
# keep or delete the old PVCs deliberately, they hold the HA recorder database
helm install hotloop ./charts/hotloop -n hotloop
```

Things that no longer exist and will be rejected if set: `sidecarProxy`,
`homeassistant`, `mqtt`/`nodered`/`esphome`/`zigbee2mqtt`
add-ons, `devices`, `cameras`, `customConfig`, `network.hostNetwork`.

## Rolling back an update

`helm rollback hotloop -n hotloop` puts the previous release's image back. It
does not put the database back: a release migrates on start, and that stays done.
This is safe because migrations only add (a table, a column with a default, an
index, never a drop, a rename or a type change), so the previous release works on
the schema the newer one left, and `test/prevrelease.sh` proves it on the real
previous image before each release ships. The rule and the check are in
[MIGRATIONS.md](/iot/migrations/).

It is safe for one release back. The database records which release applied each
migration, and a release that finds migrations from two or more releases newer than
itself refuses to start:

```
refusing to start: this database's schema is more than one release ahead of
HotLoop 4.18.3. ...
```

That is not a fault to work around. It means the database has moved further than
this release was ever run against. Roll forward to a release that knows the
schema, which is the newest one, or restore a backup taken by the release you
are on ([BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/)). Exactly one release back starts, with a warning in
the log naming both versions. Take a backup before you upgrade; the rollback
can't undo data the newer release wrote.

## Verifying an install

```bash
kubectl -n hotloop get pods
kubectl -n hotloop logs deploy/hotloop | head -20
```

A healthy start says the protocols it speaks, applies the migrations, reports
the history mode, and warns about anything worth knowing:

```
msg=starting version=4.0.0 protocols="[ethernet-ip http modbus mqtt mtconnect opcua s7comm]"
msg="writes are ENABLED: the UI, API, automations and MCP can all command devices"
msg="tag_history promoted to a hypertable" timescale=2.30.1
msg="history schema ready" mode=timescale
msg=listening addr=:8080 mcp=/mcp writes=true
```

Then check the labels the dashboard needs. This is the check that catches drift, assert the **set**, not the count, because a count check passes while the set is
wrong:

```bash
kubectl -n hotloop get svc <release> -o json \
  | jq -r '.metadata.labels | keys[] | select(startswith("embernet.ai/"))'
```

Exactly four, on the Service and on the pod:

```
embernet.ai/app-name
embernet.ai/gui-port
embernet.ai/gui-type
embernet.ai/store-app
```

If the app is running but missing from Running Apps, the Service labels are the
first place to look, the dashboard queries Services by `embernet.ai/store-app`.

A deploy from the App Store adds five more, from the `tenantLabels` the
dashboard passes: `embernet.ai/tenant`, `app-id`, `source`, `deployed-by` and
`deployment-id`. They go on every resource the chart renders and on the gateway
pod. The dashboard reads the tenant off the Service and nowhere else, so a
store-deployed Gateway without `embernet.ai/tenant` on its Service belongs to
nobody. A plain `helm install` renders none of the five.

## Probes

- `/healthz`, liveness. Answers while the process is up.
- `/readyz`, readiness. Additionally requires the database, so a pod that has
  lost its historian stops taking traffic rather than serving a UI that cannot
  answer anything.

The startup probe allows two minutes, because a first install runs migrations
and the liveness probe must not kill it mid-migration.

## Shutdown

`terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45`. On SIGTERM the app stops accepting
requests, then drains the historian queue so readings already taken are written
rather than thrown away. Cutting the grace period too short loses whatever was
in flight.

## Troubleshooting

**A device sits in `connecting`.** Look at `lastError` on the device card. Most
often a firewall between the pod and the equipment, or the wrong port. Egress is
unrestricted by the chart, so a NetworkPolicy blocking it is something else on
the cluster.

**Tags read bad quality.** The device answered but the point did not.
For Modbus, check the address base, `oneBased` if your drawings use 40001
numbering. For OPC UA, check the node id resolved; prefer the `nsu=` form.

**Values look plausible but wrong.** On Modbus, that is word order, try `CDAB`.
This is the failure that does not announce itself, because the number is not
obviously wrong.

**Nothing is being historised.** Check the Protocols screen diagnostics.
`filtered` counts readings suppressed by deadband, which is working as intended;
`dropped` counts readings lost because the database could not keep up, which is
not.

**MCP returns 401.** The bearer token. Read it from the release Secret.

**Every `/api/` request returns 401.** Expected once `auth.enabled` is true and
nobody has logged in yet, that is the point of 4.4.0. Read the generated admin
password from the release Secret (see [Auth](#auth)) and log in through the UI,
or `POST /api/auth/login` directly. See [docs/AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/).

**Lost the admin password and there is no other admin account.** Generate a new
hash and patch the Secret, then restart the pod so it re-reads the environment, `EnsureAdminUser` will not touch an account that already exists, so this
replaces the row directly rather than going through the chart:

```bash
hotloop hash-password -password 'a-new-one'
kubectl exec -n hotloop deploy/hotloop -- \
  psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c \
  "UPDATE users SET password_hash = '<the hash>' WHERE username = 'admin'"
```

**An automation is enabled but not running.** It failed to compile. The
Automations screen shows it as NOT ARMED with the reason, and the system log has
the error.
